
# Related literature {#sec-literature}

This paper draws on four bodies of work that rarely meet: the task-based economics of technology and the exposure scores built from it; field and experimental studies of generative AI at work; the psychology of reliance on algorithms and automation; and the asset-pricing literature on how markets value a firm's exposure to a technology or a risk. Each strand closes with the point at which this paper departs from it, and the section ends with the paper's data source, the Anthropic Economic Index (AEI); results begin in @sec-rq1.

## Tasks and exposure measurement

The task approach treats an occupation as a bundle of tasks and asks which of them a technology can perform. @autor2003skill classify work by its routine and non-routine content and argue that computer capital substitutes for routine tasks while complementing non-routine analytical and interactive ones, so that a technology's reach is read at the level of the task rather than the job. @acemoglu2019automation formalise the same unit: automation moves tasks from labour to capital, while the creation of new tasks returns work to labour, and the net balance depends on both margins. The task, not the occupation, is therefore the natural place to measure what a technology does.

A second generation of papers turns that framework into exposure scores. @webb2020impact measures exposure by the textual overlap between patents and the task descriptions of occupations. @felten2021occupational build the AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) index by linking measured progress in a set of AI applications to the abilities that O*NET records for each occupation, and aggregate it to industries and regions. @eloundou2024gpts rate O*NET tasks by whether access to a large language model, alone or with software built on it, could substantially reduce the time a task takes, using both human annotators and a model as raters. These measures share a design choice: they describe what the technology *could* do to a task, judged from text, abilities or rubrics, before or without observing its use.

This paper takes the task as its unit as well, but measures what is observed rather than what is possible. Its behavioural outcomes are shares of conversations matched to O*NET tasks, and its industry indices aggregate observed usage, delegation and augmentation through occupational employment weights (@sec-data). The theoretical scores enter as benchmarks: AIOE as the pre-period control in the market tests and the Eloundou ratings as the "could" side of the descriptive comparison in @sec-rq2.

## Generative AI at work

A fast-growing empirical literature measures what happens when generative AI is introduced into real work. @brynjolfsson2025generative study the staggered introduction of a generative AI assistant to customer-support agents at a large firm and find productivity gains that are largest for less experienced agents. @noy2023experimental randomise access to a chatbot among professionals performing writing tasks and find that access shortened the time taken and raised the rated quality of the output. @dellacqua2023navigating run a field experiment with management consultants and describe a "jagged technological frontier": on tasks inside the frontier AI assistance improved performance, while on a task chosen to lie outside it, participants using AI were more likely to reach an incorrect answer. They also describe distinct ways of working with the model, some participants dividing tasks between themselves and the model and others interleaving their work with it closely.

These studies measure outcomes for a defined population, a firm or an experimental sample, under controlled or quasi-random assignment. They are informative about productivity in particular settings and silent on how use is distributed across the economy's many tasks. This paper reverses the trade-off. It has no outcome measure and no assignment; it observes, across a very wide range of tasks and several releases, *how* conversations are conducted, in particular whether the task is handed over or worked through jointly. The collaboration mode that the field studies observe for a few tasks is, in the AEI, recorded for all of them. The paper accordingly makes no productivity claim and no claim about the people behind the conversations; its RQ1 results (@sec-rq1) describe usage only.

## Algorithm aversion, appreciation and trust calibration

The behavioural hypotheses of RQ1 come from the literature on when people rely on automated judgement, which PAP §1 names for each hypothesis. @dietvorst2015algorithm show that people who see an algorithm make errors become less willing to use it than a human forecaster, even when the algorithm is the more accurate of the two. @logg2019algorithm report the opposite tendency in other settings: lay participants weighted advice more when it was attributed to an algorithm than to a person, a pattern that weakened among experts. Reliance on algorithms is thus neither uniformly low nor uniformly high; it varies with the decision maker and the setting.

The human-factors literature frames the same question as one of calibration. @parasuraman1997humans distinguish use, misuse (over-reliance), disuse (under-use) and abuse of automation. @lee2004trust define appropriate reliance as trust that matches the system's capability, and describe trust as something that develops with experience of the system's performance. H1 reads the aversion literature at the level of tasks: delegation should be lower for tasks that require more education and in higher-wage occupations, where the stakes of a task are higher. H2 reads the calibration literature over time: within a task, delegation should rise across releases as experience with the model accumulates. H3 reads the misuse literature: the validation pattern, in which the person checks the model's output, should be more prevalent in occupations where errors are costly.

The departure here is one of scale and of what is observed. The aversion and appreciation studies are laboratory or online experiments with controlled stimuli and measured accuracy; the calibration literature is largely about operators of specific automated systems. This paper observes neither the accuracy of the model nor the beliefs of the user. It asks only whether the prevalence of delegation and validation across tasks, occupations and releases follows the pattern these theories predict, and it tests each prediction under a pre-registered decision rule (@sec-methods; @sec-app-pap). A pattern consistent with a theory is not evidence of its mechanism, a limit stated in @sec-limitations.

## Asset pricing of technology exposure and text-based measurement

A finance literature asks whether markets price a firm's exposure to a new technology. @eisfeldt2023generative construct firm-level exposure to generative AI from the occupational composition of firms' workforces, using task-level exposure assessments, and study how firm values moved around the public release of ChatGPT; their exposure measure, like those above, describes what the technology could do. Return tests of this kind rest on the standard tools of empirical asset pricing: the five-factor model of @fama2015five for risk adjustment, which this paper extends with the momentum factor of @carhart1997persistence, and the cross-sectional regressions of @fama1973risk for relating characteristics to average returns. A parallel literature measures firm exposure from text. @hassan2019firm build a firm-level measure of political risk from the share of earnings-call discussion devoted to political topics, an approach that treats what a firm's managers say as a measurable signal of what the firm faces.

This paper's market tests differ in three ways. Their exposure variable is built from observed delegation rather than theoretical capability, and H5b asks whether it carries information beyond a theoretical score (AIOE) that predates the release of ChatGPT on {{< var design.seal_date >}}. Their unit is the industry, because AEI usage is matched to tasks and occupations and reaches firms only through employment weights. And they are confirmatory: the specification, the null, the inference and the decision rule were fixed in the pre-analysis plan before any return dated after the seal was read, which closes for the post-seal test the search over specifications that can inflate apparent findings in return studies [@romano2005stepwise; @bailey2014deflated], although the null was recentred after pre-seal rejection rates were seen (@sec-methods; @sec-app-disclosures). The text-based strand enters through H6, which is exploratory: it compares what industries' 10-K filings say about AI with what their tasks' observed usage shows, in the spirit of @hassan2019firm, and the comparison is reported without a rejection claim (@sec-markets).

## The Anthropic Economic Index

The AEI is the paper's source of observed usage. @handa2025economic describe the method: a privacy-preserving analysis of millions of conversations with Claude, in which each conversation is matched to O*NET tasks and classified by its collaboration pattern, distinguishing automative use, where the task is handed to the model, from augmentative use, where the person iterates with it, learns from it or checks it. Later releases extend the same measurement, among them reports on uneven geographic and enterprise adoption [@appel2025uneven], on economic primitives [@appel2026economic] and on learning curves [@massenkoff2026learning], and the latest release used here [@anthropic2026economicindex]. This paper uses the published releases as inputs under a frozen plan. AEI data are conversations matched to O*NET tasks: they measure usage of Anthropic's models, not workers, jobs or outcomes, and @sec-data sets out how the releases are harmonised and what that harmonisation can and cannot support.
